# Amino Acids and Protein Structure (AAMC Category 1A)

## Classification by side chain

The twenty proteinogenic amino acids are grouped by the chemistry of their
side chains. Nonpolar side chains include glycine, alanine, valine, leucine,
isoleucine, methionine, proline, phenylalanine, and tryptophan. Polar
uncharged side chains include serine, threonine, cysteine, asparagine,
glutamine, and tyrosine.

At physiological pH, the acidic amino acids aspartate and glutamate carry a
negatively charged side chain. The basic amino acids lysine and arginine carry
a positive charge; histidine has a side chain pKa near 6.0, so it is partially
protonated at physiological pH and is the residue most often found in enzyme
active sites that shuttle protons.

## Proline and secondary structure

Proline is unique among the twenty amino acids in that its side chain bonds
back to the backbone nitrogen, forming a rigid five-membered ring. Because the
nitrogen lacks a free hydrogen once incorporated into a peptide bond, proline
cannot act as a hydrogen bond donor. This makes proline a helix breaker: it is
rarely found in the interior of an alpha helix and is common at turns.

Glycine, whose side chain is a single hydrogen atom, has the greatest
conformational freedom of any residue and is likewise common in turns.

## The isoelectric point

The isoelectric point, pI, is the pH at which an amino acid carries no net
charge. For an amino acid with a nonionizable side chain, pI is the average of
the two backbone pKa values, that of the carboxyl group and that of the amino
group. For an amino acid with an ionizable side chain, pI is the average of
the two pKa values that flank the neutral species.

## Peptide bond geometry

The peptide bond has partial double bond character arising from resonance
delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl. This restricts
rotation about the C-N bond and holds the six atoms of the peptide unit in a
single plane. The trans configuration is strongly favored over cis because the
cis arrangement places the two alpha carbons in steric conflict; the exception
is the peptide bond preceding proline, where cis and trans are closer in
energy.
